opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most misunderstood things about the economics of this industry, and I've tried to explain it a few different ways.

The way I like to think about it is: imagine each model is its own company. Say in one year you train a model that costs, I don't know, a hundred million dollars. The next year you deploy it, and it brings in, say, two or three hundred million in revenue. Looked at on its own, that model is quite profitable. It paid back its training cost and then some. But in that same year when it's bringing in revenue, you're also training the next model, and that one costs a billion dollars. Then the year after, the billion-dollar model brings in a few billion, and meanwhile you're spending ten billion on the next one.

So if you look at the company's P&L in any given year, it looks like you're losing more and more money. But if you look at it model by model, each one is a good business. The losses come from the fact that you're making an exponentially larger investment each year in the next thing. It's not that the underlying product is unprofitable. It's that you're in a phase of very rapid scaling, and the scaling itself is what's expensive.

Now, there are a couple of caveats. One is that this only works if the scaling keeps paying off, if each generation is actually enough better that customers will pay substantially more for it. I believe that's been true and I think it will continue to be true, but it is a bet. And the second is that at some point the exponential has to flatten. You can't keep spending ten times more every year forever; you run out of chips, energy, capital, or the world's GDP. When that happens, either because we hit very powerful AI or because the curve bends for some other reason, the profitability of each individual model stops being masked by the next investment, and these companies start to look extremely profitable.

The danger, and this is something I worry about a lot, is in the timing. If you're buying compute years in advance and you're off by even a year or two about how fast revenue grows, you can get into serious trouble. Data centers are committed long before you know exactly what the demand will be. So I think a lot of the craft of running one of these companies is being ambitious enough to stay at the frontier but disciplined enough that you're not betting the company on everything going perfectly. We've tried to be fairly conservative there, to plan so that even if things grow somewhat slower than the most bullish projections, we're still fine. Some others in the industry are, I think, taking bigger swings, and maybe it works out for them, but I don't think you need to YOLO it to stay at the frontier.

So the short version: the losses you see are mostly investment, not a broken business model. But investment at this scale requires being honest with yourself about uncertainty, because the downside of getting the timing wrong is quite severe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that there are really two different things going on at once, and people conflate them, which leads to a lot of confusion about whether these companies are "losing money."

The first thing is: each model, considered on its own, is actually a pretty good business. You spend, say, a hundred million dollars training a model, and then over the next year or two that model generates several hundred million dollars in revenue. If you just looked at that one model as a standalone project, you'd say the margins are fine, the return on investment is fine, this is a healthy business.

The second thing is that at the same time you're deploying that model, you're training the next one, and the next one costs ten times as much. So if you look at the company's financials in any given year, you see revenue from the previous generation of models and costs from the next generation, and because the costs are scaling faster than any single model's revenue, the company as a whole appears to be losing money. But that's an artifact of the investment curve, not of the underlying unit economics.

So the question is really: how long does that curve keep going? And there's a few scenarios. One is that the scaling continues and the models keep getting more capable and more valuable, in which case you keep reinvesting and the "losses" are really just a reflection of how much opportunity there is. The other is that at some point the returns from scaling flatten out, and at that point you stop spending ten times as much on the next model, and the business becomes profitable very quickly, because the thing you've already built keeps generating revenue.

The failure mode people worry about, and it's a legitimate thing to worry about, is the scenario where you've committed to the very large training run and then the revenue doesn't materialize to support it. So we think a lot about staging it, about making sure that the revenue from the current generation is actually there before we scale the next one, rather than just betting everything on the curve continuing. But I'd say the fundamental dynamic is that this looks like a money-losing business when it's really a very capital-intensive business with good margins where the capital intensity is growing fast.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the economics of the business you’re operating today from the investment you’re making in the next generation of models. You can have a model that earns more in revenue than it costs to serve, and you can have that business growing very quickly, while the company as a whole is losing money because you’re spending so much on research and training the next model.

The important question is what that investment buys you. If spending more produces a more capable model, and that model creates enough value that people want to pay for it, then investing ahead of revenue can make sense. In fact, becoming profitable immediately might mean you’re passing up a very large opportunity.

But that isn’t an unlimited justification for spending. You have to ask: Are customers getting real value? Are the margins on serving them good? And is each successive investment generating enough additional revenue to justify its cost? Growth and profitability aren’t opposites, but growth by itself doesn’t establish that the economics work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the profitability of the business you’re running today from the investment you’re making in the next generation of models. You can have a model that earns more revenue than it costs to serve, and still have a company that’s losing money because you’re spending a lot on training the next model and building capacity for future demand.

That doesn’t make the investment automatically justified. The question is whether those investments will produce enough future revenue to pay for themselves. If demand grows quickly, investing more can mean you become profitable later, even though the underlying business is getting stronger. But you have to keep checking that assumption. Spending a lot of money is not, by itself, evidence that you’re creating something valuable.
